speaker_role: former admissions officer (Andrew Hoffman, former Director of Admissions at Swarthmore College, former admissions officer at Vanderbilt University), now runs a paid consulting/content business
commercial_incentive: Yes - repeatedly promotes private family sessions, a junior application-materials review service, and mock interview prep at askdrhoffman.com
key_insights: Demonstrated interest matters primarily at 'target'/yield-sensitive schools trying to manage admit and yield rates, not at extremely high-demand brand-name schools that assume most admits will enroll regardless (he names Swarthmore, Columbia, Brown, Harvard as largely not tracking it)

Ranks 28 specific interest signals from weakest to strongest, e.g., social media follows and viewbook downloads are weak/low-effort; attending a high school visit by an admissions rep, a specific 'why us' supplemental essay, and campus visits are much stronger, largely because they require real effort and are reliably tracked in admissions CRMs

The single most powerful demonstrated-interest signal is applying Early Decision, since it's a binding commitment to enroll if admitted; being accepted into a college's fly-in program (an all-expenses-paid recruiting visit, mostly aimed at underrepresented/underserved students) is ranked as the second-strongest signal since the college has already invested real money specifically in that applicant

Explains that data from platforms like Scoir, Naviance, or Common App (adding a school to an 'interested' list) can sometimes flow to colleges via paid data-sharing partnerships, but this varies by vendor-college relationship and is mostly invisible to applicants

Advises checking the Common Data Set section C7 ('level of applicant's interest') to see whether a specific school self-reports tracking interest as very important, important, considered, or not considered - while cautioning that the office completing that section (often institutional research) may not perfectly reflect actual admissions office practice

States that at Swarthmore, students accepted into the fly-in program who later applied were admitted at over 75%, compared to the school's overall ~7% admit rate (though this is a self-selected group, not necessarily a causal effect of the program alone)
Warns against turning interest-demonstration into hollow performative checklisting, arguing officers can distinguish authentic engagement from strategic over-communication
specific_numbers_or_facts: Only about 65 U.S. colleges offer fly-in programs (per speaker)
At Swarthmore, fly-in program admits who applied were admitted at >75% vs. the school's overall ~7% admit rate (per speaker, from his own tenure there)
University of Chicago tracks summer program attendance specifically to offer an exclusive 'ED zero' early decision round to attendees
Common Data Set section C7 identified as the specific place to check a school's self-reported level of interest tracking
notable_or_distinctive: Extremely granular, explicitly ranked 28-item taxonomy of interest signals (from social media follows to fly-in acceptance) with a named, checkable data source (Common Data Set C7) for verifying whether a given school even tracks interest - far more specific than typical 'visit campus and email admissions' advice.
reliability_notes: Speaker has genuine former-admissions credentials (Swarthmore, Vanderbilt) lending credibility, but the ranking order is explicitly his own judgment ('may vary from college to college') rather than universal fact; some claims (CRM tracking, vendor data-sharing) are plausible industry knowledge but not independently sourced in the transcript; heavy self-promotion throughout for paid services.
